t1.label: Standard form
t1.summary: A quadratic is any equation where the highest power of x is two. Before solving, it is always written in standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0, where a must not be 0. From standard form, it can be solved by factoring, completing the square, or the quadratic formula.
keyPoints: A quadratic has x² as its highest power of x.
Standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0.
a must not be 0 (a ≠ 0), or it is not a quadratic.
Always rewrite in standard form first, before solving.
Three main methods: factoring, completing the square, quadratic formula.
t1.example: x² + 5x + 6 = 0 is in standard form with a = 1, b = 5, c = 6; it factors as (x + 2)(x + 3), giving roots x = −2 and x = −3.

t2.label: Solving methods
t2.summary: Quadratic equations (highest power of x is two) are first written in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, then solved by one of three main methods. Factoring is quickest when the expression splits nicely, completing the square works even when factoring doesn't, and the quadratic formula always works.
keyPoints: Always write the equation in standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0.
Factoring: split into two brackets; each bracket set to zero gives a root.
Completing the square: halve the b term and square it.
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, which always works.
Discriminant b² − 4ac: > 0 two real roots, = 0 one repeated root, < 0 no real roots.
Check the discriminant before solving; roots are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
t2.example: x² + 5x + 6 factors to (x + 2)(x + 3), giving roots x = −2 and x = −3. Completing the square on x² + 6x + 5 gives (x + 3)² − 4.

t3.label: Factoring
t3.summary: Factoring is the first method for solving quadratics. When the quadratic splits nicely into two brackets, it's the easiest method. Once factored, each bracket gives a root.
keyPoints: Factoring is the first solving method covered.
Works best when the quadratic splits nicely into two brackets.
x² + 5x + 6 factors to (x + 2)(x + 3).
Set each bracket to zero to find the roots.
If factoring doesn't work, completing the square still does.
t3.example: x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3), so the roots are x = −2 and x = −3.

t4.label: Completing the square
t4.summary: Completing the square is a method for solving quadratics that works even when factoring doesn't. Starting from standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, you halve the b term and square it to rewrite the expression as a squared bracket plus or minus a number.
keyPoints: First write the quadratic in standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0.
Rule of thumb: halve the b term, then square it.
Works even when factoring doesn't.
Result has the form (x + b/2)² plus or minus a constant.
t4.example: x² + 6x + 5: halve 6 to get 3, square it to get 9, so x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, giving (x + 3)² − 4 = 0.

t5.label: Quadratic formula
t5.summary: The quadratic formula, x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, solves any quadratic written in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, and it always works. The part under the square root, b² − 4ac, is called the discriminant and tells you how many real roots there are.
keyPoints: Write the equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 first.
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a — it always works.
Discriminant b² − 4ac > 0: two real roots.
Discriminant = 0: one repeated root; < 0: no real roots.
Roots are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
Always check the discriminant before you start solving.
t5.example: The parabola whose x-axis crossings give the roots is the same shape of curve a basketball follows after a jump shot.

t6.label: Discriminant
t6.summary: The discriminant is b² − 4ac, the part under the square root in the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. Its sign tells you how many real roots a quadratic in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 has, so always check it before you start solving.
keyPoints: Discriminant = b² − 4ac, the expression under the square root.
Write the equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 first.
Positive discriminant: two real roots.
Zero discriminant: one repeated root.
Negative discriminant: no real roots.
Roots are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
t6.example: The parabola's shape is the same curve a basketball follows after a jump shot; the roots are where that curve crosses the x-axis.

t7.label: Positive: two roots
t7.summary: The discriminant is the part under the square root in the quadratic formula: b² − 4ac. When it is positive (b² − 4ac > 0), the quadratic has two real roots. Graphically, this means the parabola crosses the x-axis at two points.
keyPoints: Discriminant = b² − 4ac, the part under the square root.
If b² − 4ac > 0, there are two real roots.
Roots are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
Positive discriminant: the parabola crosses the x-axis twice.
Compare: = 0 gives one repeated root; < 0 gives no real roots.

t8.label: Zero: one root
t8.summary: For a quadratic in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant is b² − 4ac, the part under the square root. When the discriminant is exactly zero, the equation has one repeated root. Graphically, the roots are where the parabola meets the x-axis, so this case gives a single meeting point.
keyPoints: Write the equation in standard form first: ax² + bx + c = 0.
The discriminant is b² − 4ac, the part under the square root.
If b² − 4ac = 0, there is one repeated root.
Compare: positive gives two real roots, negative gives no real roots.
Roots are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

t9.label: Negative: no real roots
t9.summary: The discriminant of a quadratic is b² − 4ac. When it is negative (b² − 4ac < 0), the quadratic has no real roots at all. Graphically, roots are where the parabola crosses the x axis, so a negative discriminant means the parabola never crosses it.

If b² − 4ac < 0, there are no real roots
Roots are where the parabola crosses the x axis

Compare: > 0 gives two real roots, = 0 gives one repeated root
t9.example: The parabola is the same curve a basketball follows after a jump shot; with a negative discriminant, the curve never touches the x axis.

t10.label: Parabola graphs
t10.summary: A quadratic can be drawn as a curve called a parabola. Graphically, the roots of the quadratic are the points where the parabola crosses the x-axis. The same parabola shape also describes real motion, such as the path of a thrown ball.
keyPoints: A quadratic's graph is a parabola.
Roots are the x-intercepts: where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
The parabola shape describes projectile motion, like a basketball's flight.
Babylonian scribes solved quadratics almost 4,000 years ago on clay tablets.
t10.example: A basketball after a jump shot travels along a parabola-shaped path through the air.

t11.label: Projectile motion
t11.summary: The parabola curve studied in this lecture also describes the path of a thrown object. A basketball flying after a jump shot follows this same parabolic arc.
keyPoints: A projectile's path follows the same parabola curve as these graphs.
A basketball after a jump shot travels in a parabolic arc.
